evidence.excerpt: The central problem in the epistemology of perception is that of explaining how perception could give us knowledge or justified belief about an external world, about things outside of ourselves.

Two main types of response to the skeptical argument have traditionally been given: a metaphysical response that focuses on the nature of the world, perceptual experience, and/or the relation between them, in an effort to show that perceptual knowledge is indeed possible; and a more directly epistemological response

Additionally, the direct realist is free to impose a metaevidential demand on justified perceptual belief, a demand that we know which kind of experience we are having before that experience can serve as evidence.
An entirely metaphysical solution to the problem of the external world will not suffice.
Any satisfactory, non-skeptical epistemology of perception is going to deny one or more of the epistemological premises of PEW.

The first two are normally defended as parts of and continuous with a more general epistemological view, encompassing not just perception but also testimony, introspection, memory, inductive and deductive inference, and so on.
The pioneer of this general approach is John McDowell (1982), although it is difficult to know just what view he endorses.
A second motivation is the claim that some or all evidence is factive.
Principle, at least in a form that holds that the metaevidential knowledge/justification is prior to the perceptual knowledge/justification.

sources.annotation: Distinguishes epistemic from metaphysical directness and surveys evidential, etiological, and world-involving justification.
